title: Does adoption spread through village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed?
summary: Research programme on the 43 Karnataka village networks of Banerjee, Chandrasekhar, Duflo and Jackson (2013; CC0 replication data, 9,126 households, 44,367 ties): can cross-sectional adoption data tell a simple contagion from a complex one, and which seeding rule stays near the best under every model the data cannot reject? Milestone 1 ports the authors’ estimation code (information model, five moments, identity weights, their 31 × 39 grid, Bayesian bootstrap). It reproduces the data (non-leader take-up 18.7% vs 18.5% published, leaders 24.7% vs 24.8%), q<sub>P</sub> > q<sub>N</sub> (98.4% of 1,000 bootstrap draws) and the counterfactual (take-up falls by 0.337 with non-adopters silent; paper 0.32), but not the published point: the minimum is q<sub>N</sub> = 0.05, q<sub>P</sub> = 0.30 for three seeds against 0.10, 0.50, which scores 11 times our minimum; q<sub>P</sub> is weakly identified (95% interval 0.15–1.0) and moves to 0.15–0.25 with two-step weights or quarterly periods. Milestone 2 fits two complex-contagion models on the same information spread, a reinforcement model (logit gains γ per adopting neighbour) and a fractional threshold, and compares them leaving one village out. Both fit better in sample (reinforcement γ = 0.10, positive in 99.5% of 1,000 bootstrap draws, criterion 41% lower; this fine-grid, free-intercept fit is post hoc, the pre-registered coarse grid gave γ = 0) yet predict held-out villages worse than the simple model (better in 13 and 19 of 43; in 12% and 24% of paired bootstrap draws). Take-up by adopting neighbours, 8.3% with none to 35.0% with four or more, is more convex than the simple model's 8.1% to 27.2%, a shape reinforcement, homophily or degree could each leave. Milestone 3 simulates 200 datasets from each fitted model on the real networks and refits all three: in sample the criterion picks the reinforcement model for 85% of datasets the simple model made; leaving one village out recovers the true model 58.5%, 82% and 55.5% of the time (simple, threshold, reinforcement), so milestone 2’s verdict is weak evidence. The moment map’s weakest direction trades the base adoption rate against word of mouth and reinforcement (condition number 79). A post-hoc check finds the real villages’ held-out errors two to four times larger than any model produces in its own synthetic data: every model is too homogeneous across villages. Milestone 3b adds a village random effect on the base adoption rate, identified by the squared village take-up rate: it is not needed (σ-hat = 0 in every family; the information model’s own word-of-mouth randomness already matches how much take-up varies between villages) and it does not close the gap (no synthetic dataset from the information or reinforcement model reaches the real held-out error). A threshold model with a free intercept does reach it (19% of its synthetic datasets) and now predicts held-out villages best (loss 0.169 against 0.181 and 0.210). The misfit is in where adopters sit, not how many: 57% of the real error is one moment, own adoption times second-neighbour adopters (a quirk of the original code), which a cascade model reproduces and a per-household-chance model cannot. Milestone 4 scores ten seeding rules at the leaders’ budget under all three fitted models: the advice barely depends on which model is right. Greedy seeding under the threshold model loses at most 0.5% of adopters against the best rule under every model (minimax-regret in 94% of bootstrap draws), the structural rules rank almost identically (Kendall τ 0.81–1.0), top degree loses 2–4%, the lender’s leaders 6–10%. Clustered seeds do not help even under the threshold model: one clustered patch is about as bad as random, and the best seeds have moderate degree and are rarely neighbours. Point fits, a fixed budget and no homophily; a model’s counterfactual, not a field result. Milestone 5 asks what a rollout without a fitted model or a full census gives up: degree discount (Chen, Wang and Yang 2009) loses at most 1.4% under every fitted model and beats top degree in every bootstrap draw, while forbidding adjacent seeds alone loses 3.4% because it drops seed degree to 13; surveying a random 25% of households and seeding top estimated degree loses at most 4.5% (90% interval 1.7–9.7%), 10% loses 6.7%, and friend nomination (no network data) loses 6.2% against 12.1% for random seeds. Milestone 6 scores the rules over a village bootstrap that refits all three models in every draw (205 distinct fitted processes; the information model’s fit moves off its point estimate in 93% of draws): degree discount’s median worst-case regret is 1.0% (5–95%: 0.3–1.6%), it beats top degree in all 500 draws, and its one rate parameter barely matters (0.9–1.2% for any p from 0.01 to 0.15). Parameter uncertainty widens the model-specific greedy rules’ tails (greedy under the threshold model 0.1–2.4%, under the information model up to 7.3%) but not degree discount’s. Scoring randomised rules on independent runs moves milestone 5’s 25% survey result from 4.5% to 5.0–5.1%, at its 5% bar. Milestone 7 adds complex centrality (Guilbeault and Centola 2021), the measure built for complex contagions: its best version (absolute threshold 2) loses at most 3.7% of adopters (top degree 4.1%, degree discount 1.4%, which beats it in every bootstrap draw); at a fractional threshold of one half it is mostly degree; and seeding whole neighbourhoods, as the measure presumes, loses 10–13%, about as much as random seeds. Milestone 8 rescores the complex-centrality rules over milestone 6’s 500 refitted bootstrap draws: degree discount still beats every one of them in every draw; the absolute-2 version (median worst case 3.3%, 5–95%: 2.4–5.3%) beats top degree in 74% of draws, and under the threshold model its loss falls as the refitted threshold rises (4.9% at θ = 0.4, 2.7% at 0.6), the direction its theory predicts, yet never down to degree discount’s. Milestone 9 asks whether a partial network survey can stand in for a census: surveying half the households at random, then the households they named most, and ranking by degree discount on the ties seen loses 1.6% under the worst fitted model (census degree discount 1.4%; the same ranking on a random half 3.3%); the adaptive second stage does not help top-estimated-degree ranking (5.9% against 5.2% on a quarter), and the best quarter-sample rule (4.5%) stays just above census top degree (4.1%). Milestone 10 rescores those survey rules over the 500 refitted bootstrap draws: the half survey loses a median 1.9% (5–95%: 1.0–3.3%) against 1.1% for census degree discount and beats census top degree in 97% of draws; spending three quarters of it at random and a quarter on the most-named households lowers that to 1.5%, and the adaptive stage beats a plain random sample in 89–93% of draws. Milestone 11 measures how many ties a respondent names, by capture–recapture on the survey’s converse questions (borrow from / lend to, visit / invite): about 84% for three questions together (68–83% for one). At that recall the three-quarters-random half survey loses a median 1.8% (census degree discount with the same forgetting 1.4%, census top degree 4.1%), and with half of all ties forgotten degree discount on a census still beats top degree on a perfect census in 99% of draws. Milestone 12 asks whether respondents forget weak ties more: stratified by how many other survey questions name the same pair, recall is 61% for ties no other question names, 81% for one and 94% for two or more, so the pooled 84% was only a little high (stratified 81%). Under that uneven forgetting the half survey loses a median 2.2% (beating census top degree in 98% of draws) and census degree discount within a point of a perfect census. Milestone 13 gives every randomised rule its own scoring stream and re-draws four rules five times: the apparent census gain from uneven forgetting (0.9% against 1.8%) is Monte Carlo noise (mean gap −0.07 point over five copies), and a randomised rule’s joint median moves by up to 0.47 point (sd) between copies, so sub-point differences between randomised rules in milestones 10 to 12 are within noise; the survey advice (about 2%) is unchanged. Milestone 14 re-draws 16 randomised rules five times and pools the copies (500 survey draws per village), putting a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.03–0.24 point on each: forgetting half the ties now costs more than forgetting a quarter (milestone 11’s non-monotone recall was noise), the three ways of splitting a half survey are within 0.4 point and not ranked (three quarters random 1.79%, one quarter 1.81%, half 2.17%), the half survey at the measured recall loses a median 2.2% and beats census top degree in 97% of draws, and a single copy biases every worst-case regret up by about 0.15 point. Milestone 15 fills in the recall range a field team works in (0.7 to 0.9) with ten Monte Carlo copies of three rules (se 0.10–0.16 point): no rule scores worse with more recall in any adjacent pair beyond 2 se, milestone 14’s apparent dip for census degree discount at 0.85 was noise (+0.12 point, se 0.15; the first five copies ran high), census rules are flat across the range (top degree 4.2–4.3%, degree discount 1.4–1.6%), and the half survey improves by 0.21 point per 0.1 of recall (se 0.07), from 2.39% at 0.7 to 1.81% at 0.9, beating census top degree in at least 97% of draws at every level. Milestone 16 adds false ties, swept because the archive cannot measure them: at 85% recall plus up to one false tie per four true ones, census degree discount loses 1.6–1.9% and the half survey 2.2–2.7%, both beating a perfect census ranked by top degree in 95–99% of draws; false ties placed at random cost nothing measurable, while false ties that close triangles cost every rule more (top degree 0.8 point at one per four, z 3.5; census degree discount 2.8% and the half survey 2.9% at one per two). Milestone 17 tests the field fix, keeping only ties both ends name: on a census it removes the triangle-closing cost (census degree discount 2.8% to 2.2% at one false tie per two, z 2.6; top degree 5.1% to 4.6%, z 2.4) and leaves both rules flat in the false-tie rate, for about 0.2 point of lost recall when there are no false ties; on the half survey, where most ties cannot be checked, it saves nothing and costs 0.2–0.5 point under random false ties, so a census should be filtered and a partial survey should not. Milestone 18 drops that milestone’s best-case assumption, that each end invents a false tie on its own: when a share κ of false ties is named by both ends (and so survives the filter), the filter’s gain for census degree discount shrinks from 0.60 point at κ = 0 to 0.39 at 0.25, turns into a cost by κ ≈ 0.4–0.5, and costs 0.5–0.6 point at κ = 1 (z 3.0 to 7.9), five times its recall cost with no false ties; census top degree never pays for it measurably. So the filter helps a census only if false ties are mostly one-sided, which reciprocity itself cannot reveal. Recall is independent across the two ends of a tie within a strength stratum, the strength measure is a proxy, and the false-tie rate and its proportionality to degree are assumed and swept, not measured.
lede: research programme: does adoption spread through real village networks as a simple or a complex contagion, and whom should a rollout seed? On the 43 Banerjee et al. (2013) microfinance villages, the data cannot reliably tell the models apart, but the seeding advice survives that and the uncertainty in the fits: degree discount, which needs the network but no model, loses a median 1.0% of adopters (at most 1.6% in 95% of refitted bootstrap draws) under every fitted model, greedy seeding 0.5%, a 25% household survey about 5% (a two-stage survey of half the households, ranked by degree discount on the ties seen, 1.6% at the point fits, a median 1.9% over refitted fits, and 1.8% for its three-quarters-random split when respondents forget the 16% of ties measured in the same survey, 2.2% when, as measured, they forget weak ties four times as often as strong ones, 1.8 to 2.4% for any recall from 70% to 90%, and 2.2 to 2.7% when respondents also name one false tie per four true ones; keeping only ties both ends name helps a census, not a half survey, and stops helping once about half of false ties are named by both ends), the lender's leaders 6 to 10%, and clustering seeds together does not help; complex centrality, the measure built for complex contagions, loses up to 3.7% (a median 3.3% over refitted fits; it helps more the higher the fitted threshold, but never matches degree discount), and seeding whole neighbourhoods 10 to 13%.
